CausalChain: High-fat diet/obesity -> Gut microbiota dysbiosis -> Increased production of hydrophobic secondary bile acids (e.g. DCA, LCA) -> Activation of bile acid receptors (TGR5, FXR) in colonic epithelial cells -> Dysregulation of apoptotic and proliferative signaling and modulation of epigenetic regulators (e.g. inhibition of HDACs, increased nuclear sphingosine-1-phosphate) -> Induction of cancer stem cell features -> Promotion of colorectal carcinogenesis
Hypothesis: Altered gut microbiota following a high-fat diet increases levels of hydrophobic secondary bile acids, which via TGR5 and FXR‐mediated epigenetic reprogramming induce a cancer stem cell phenotype in colonic epithelial cells, thereby driving colorectal cancer initiation and progression.
Abstract: We propose that progressive changes in gut microbial composition, often observed in states of high‐fat feeding and obesity, lead to an increased production of hydrophobic secondary bile acids such as deoxycholic acid and lithocholic acid. These metabolites, at physiological concentrations, activate cell–surface and nuclear receptor cascades (including TGR5 and FXR) in colonic epithelial cells. Such receptor activation results in a dysregulation of apoptotic and proliferative signaling, while also triggering epigenetic modulators such as altered histone deacetylase activity, ultimately leading to the emergence of cancer stem cell‐like phenotypes. This cascade of events may be a key initiating mechanism in colorectal carcinogenesis. Based on this, we hypothesize that interventions aimed at modulating the microbiome or blocking the receptor–dependent epigenetic reprogramming could reverse or mitigate the tumorigenic process in the colon.
